extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning proof techniques / discrete mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Worked solutions and methodological guidance for elementary proof-writing in discrete mathematics (number theory, sets, relations, induction). Shows which proof techniques to use and how to apply them to typical exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use direct proof
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove an implication, assume the antecedent and derive the consequent by stepwise algebraic or logical manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Suppose x is even, write x = 2n and compute 3x+5 = 6n+5 = 2(3n+2)+1 to show odd; show a = 14m implies 7|a and 2|a by writing a = 7(2m) and a = 2(7m). Often used in parity and divisibility problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contrapositive proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove an implication P => Q by proving its contrapositive (not Q) => (not P).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text uses contrapositive repeatedly (e.g., show 'if a^3 + a^2 + a is even then a is even' by assuming a is odd and deriving a^3 + a^2 + a is odd). Often helpful when the direct route is awkward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use proof by contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume the negation of the desired conclusion (or assume hypothesis plus negation) and derive a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used for irrationality arguments and impossibility claims (e.g., assume rationality of r + √2 leads to √2 rational); also used in divisibility/prime-difference contradictions. Explicit pattern: suppose contrary and reach an impossible inequality or parity contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use cases (case analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Split the argument into exhaustive cases (e.g., parity: even/odd; sign: positive/negative; one variable zero) and prove the statement in each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many proofs use 'Case 1/Case 2' structure (e.g., if x=0 or y=0; if n odd or even). Combine with WLOG to reduce symmetric cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mathematical induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove a statement for all n∈N by verifying base case(s) and proving that truth for k implies truth for k+1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard template: base case, assume for k, show for k+1 by algebraic manipulation (examples: sum of first n integers, sum of cubes, power/divisibility inductive proofs). Show how to set S and manipulate (e.g., multiply by 2, subtract) to derive closed forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use strong induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume statement holds for all values up to k and use that to prove it for k+1; useful when proof for k+1 requires multiple prior instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied for statements about intersections/unions over many sets (the page explicitly uses strong induction for n-set identity). State induction hypothesis for ≤k and extend to k+1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate remainders / modular arithmetic (parity and mod 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use residues modulo small integers (2,4, etc.) to rule out possibilities or classify forms (e.g., squares mod 4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint: 'investigate the remainders of a sum of squares (mod 4)'. Remark: 'two more than a perfect square is always either 2 (mod 4) or 3 (mod 4)'. Apply to show impossibility of integer solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisibility manipulations (write b = a k)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a|b or deduce consequences, express divisibility by introducing an integer multiplier (b = a·k) and manipulate algebraically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used throughout: e.g., show a|k => a|k^2, prove subsets of multiples sets by writing elements as 12n = 2(6n) = 3(4n), or show if a|k then a|k^2. Useful in proving set inclusions like {12n} ⊆ {2n} ∩ {3n}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Element-chasing to prove set inclusion and equality
rubrics_metrics.description: To show A⊆B, take arbitrary a∈A and show a∈B; for equality show both A⊆B and B⊆A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many set proofs use this pattern verbatim ('Suppose a∈... Then ... therefore a∈...'). Use double inclusion to establish equality (explicitly done for several identities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use De Morgan's laws and complement manipulation for set identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Transform complements and unions/intersections via De Morgan to simplify and prove identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: proofs that A−(B∪C) = (A−B)∩(A−C) and that A∪B = (U−(A∩B)) etc. Work through element definitions then apply De Morgan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove biconditional (iff) statements by proving both directions
rubrics_metrics.description: For 'P iff Q' prove P=>Q and Q=>P separately, choosing appropriate proof methods for each direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common pattern: one direction via contrapositive, the other via direct proof or case analysis (examples: parity equivalences and even/odd sum results).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide counterexamples to disprove universal claims
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a universally quantified statement is false, exhibit a single explicit counterexample and explain why it violates the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disproofs in the text give concrete small-number counterexamples (e.g., for inequalities or set equalities). State values, compute both sides, conclude falsehood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use explicit factorization/algebraic identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply algebraic factorizations (e.g., (x+y)^n expansion, x^3−y^3=(x−y)(x^2+xy+y^2)) to transform expressions into useful forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in proving monotonicity of cube (x^3−y^3 factorization) and binomial theorem (induction step expansion). Use identity to factor differences and deduce sign or divisibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify relation properties (reflexive, symmetric, transitive) directly
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a relation is an equivalence, check reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity by direct computation or algebraic manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: show x−x∈Z for reflexivity, use negation for symmetry (if x−y∈Z then y−x=−(x−y)∈Z), and add integer differences for transitivity. For arithmetic divisibility relations, manipulate linear combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute equivalence classes by solving defining condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an equivalence relation, characterize [a] = {x : xRa} by simplifying the criterion (often reduces to parity or residue classes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: relation 3x−5y even yields two classes (even and odd); 4|(x+3y) yields residue-class descriptions like [0]={multiples of 4}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'without loss of generality' (WLOG) to reduce symmetric cases
rubrics_metrics.description: When two cases are symmetric interchangeably, assume one ordering to avoid redundant work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in parity proofs where 'without loss of generality, let a be even and b odd' to simplify argument. Ensure symmetry justification is stated or obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct explicit examples to prove existence statements
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove existence, provide an explicit element satisfying the property rather than abstract argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: showing there is a prime between 90 and 100 by pointing out 97 is prime; showing intersection nonempty by presenting pq in both generated sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sum manipulation techniques (telescoping, multiply-and-subtract)
rubrics_metrics.description: Manipulate finite sums by forming related sums (e.g., multiply by constant, shift index, subtract) to obtain closed forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: geometric series S = 2^0 + ... + 2^n, multiply by 2 and subtract to get S = 2^{n+1}−1; telescoping series used in some inductive sums.
